strategy:
1. Approach and rationale
Use a feasible direct-search algorithm built from pairwise mass transfers, with occasional random zero-sum directions and seeded restarts. Along any fixed direction, every lag contribution is exactly a quadratic in the step length. Search that one-dimensional feasible interval using a deterministic coarse grid followed by local grid refinement, then accept a move only after recomputing the evaluator’s exact full-correlation score. Pairwise transfers preserve the mass constraint, while joint capped-simplex projection protects every candidate against floating-point drift.

This is materially different from the previous approach: it does not use log-sum-exp continuation, SLSQP, or a nonlinear epigraph solve. It uses no smooth surrogate or general-purpose optimizer; its primary operation is direct search along feasible directions using the exact lag formulas. The justified facts are that the finite full correlation has the lag representation below, each directional restriction is quadratic, and projection onto the box-constrained mass hyperplane has a monotone scalar solution. The heuristic is that coordinate exchanges, random directions, and restarts may improve the supplied construction. This is a local heuristic: finite line grids can miss narrow minima, nonconvexity can leave other basins unexplored, and no global optimum or bound of 0.3808 is guaranteed.

2. Mathematical specification
For n samples define dx = 2/n, T = n/2, and h = (h₀,…,hₙ₋₁). Feasibility is 0 ≤ hᵢ ≤ 1 and Σᵢ hᵢ = T, which is exactly the stated discretized integral constraint dx Σᵢ hᵢ = 1. Do not change the parent’s resolution.

Use every integer lag d from −(n−1) through n−1. Let I_d contain the integers i satisfying 0 ≤ i < n and 0 ≤ i+d < n; equivalently, max(0,−d) ≤ i ≤ min(n−1,n−1−d). Define
c_d(h) = dx Σ_{i∈I_d} h_{i+d}(1−hᵢ), and F(h) = max_d c_d(h).
The authoritative score is exactly max(np.correlate(h, 1−h, mode='full') * dx). Its 2n−1 entries include both lag directions and the shortened finite-boundary overlaps. Do not use circular correlation, omit nonzero lags, or substitute an autocorrelation identity that drops boundary terms.

For coordinate k, the derivative of the scaled lag contribution is
G[d,k] = dx × ( 1_{0≤k−d<n}(1−h_{k−d}) − 1_{0≤k+d<n}h_{k+d} ),
where a term with a false indicator is zero. This follows by differentiating h_{i+d}(1−hᵢ) with respect to either factor and includes both contributions when d=0.

For a direction v with Σᵢvᵢ=0, let h(α)=h+αv. Each lag is exactly
c_d(h(α)) = a_d + b_d α + q_d α²,
where a_d=c_d(h), b_d=dx Σ_{i∈I_d}[v_{i+d}(1−hᵢ)−h_{i+d}vᵢ], and q_d=−dx Σ_{i∈I_d}v_{i+d}vᵢ. Thus the exact line objective is max_d(a_d+b_dα+q_dα²), not a Taylor approximation.

For a pair transfer v=e_p−e_q with p<q, the feasible interval is lo=max(−h_p,h_q−1) and hi=min(1−h_p,h_q). Its linear coefficient is b=G[:,p]−G[:,q]. Its quadratic coefficients are q₀=−2dx, q_{q−p}=q_{−(q−p)}=dx, and zero at all other lags. For a general zero-sum v, calculate b and q from the sums above; equivalently, in NumPy correlation order, b = dx × (correlate(v,1−h) − correlate(h,v)) and q = −dx × correlate(v,v), all with mode='full'. For a general direction, compute the feasible alpha interval by intersecting each coordinate’s interval from 0 ≤ hᵢ+αvᵢ ≤ 1.

Joint feasibility restoration is Euclidean projection onto {x : 0≤xᵢ≤1, Σxᵢ=T}. Its form is xᵢ=clip(yᵢ−λ,0,1), where λ is chosen so Σᵢclip(yᵢ−λ,0,1)=T. The sum is continuous and nonincreasing in λ, so bisection followed by a small residual correction enforces both constraints jointly. Do not clip and then rescale.

Two useful restart transformations preserve the exact score: complementing h maps c_d to c_{−d}, and reversing the sample order also reverses the lag ordering. A circular roll is not an invariance under finite boundaries; use it only as a different starting point and always score it with the original finite correlation.

3. Implementation procedure
3.1. Define run(seed=42, **kwargs) and every helper at module top level; do not use nested functions or lambdas. Use NumPy float64 and the allowed standard numerical libraries, but no optimizer is required. Do not use filesystem or network I/O, print results, redefine initial_h_values, or serialize its entries. Compute the score directly rather than depending on an undocumented signature for evaluate_erdos_solution.

3.2. At runtime, read initial_h_values from the global namespace if it exists. Convert it to a float64 array inside a try/except. Treat it as a usable parent only if conversion succeeds, it is one-dimensional, nonempty, and entirely finite. Copy it before any modification. Its length determines n and is authoritative. If the parent already satisfies the box and mass constraints within 1e−10, preserve its values as the first start and immutable fallback. Otherwise, jointly project it and use that feasible projection as the first start and fallback. Never truncate, interpolate, or otherwise change a valid parent’s resolution.

If no usable parent exists, use n=47 unless kwargs contains an integer n_points in [1,64]; in that case use that requested value. Initialize the fallback to the feasible uniform vector filled with 0.5. Set T=n/2 and dx=2.0/n. If a valid parent has n>64, still preserve its resolution, project and score its fallback, but skip the pair-search stages to avoid an expensive exhaustive exchange search. For n=1, return the feasible fallback without search. Convert seed to an integer and reduce it modulo 2³²; if conversion fails, use 42. Create one numpy.random.default_rng instance and use it for all deterministic seeded choices.

3.3. Implement a top-level capped-simplex projection helper taking a finite vector y and T. Reject a wrong-shaped or nonfinite candidate so the caller can skip it. If a finite input has maximum absolute magnitude greater than 1e12, return the uniform feasible vector to avoid unsafe arithmetic. Otherwise set low=min(y)−1 and high=max(y); at low the clipped sum is n and at high it is zero. Perform 100 bisection steps using a midpoint computed without summing two potentially large endpoints. If sum(clip(y−mid,0,1)) > T, raise low to mid; otherwise lower high to mid. Form x=clip(y−(low+high)/2,0,1).

Compute residual r=T−sum(x). If r>0, traverse coordinates in increasing index order and add min(r,1−xᵢ) to each until the residual is negligible. If r<0, subtract min(−r,xᵢ) in the same way. Recompute the residual and make one further adjustment on a coordinate with sufficient slack if possible. Check finiteness, exact box bounds, and |sum(x)−T|≤1e−10. If numerical correction fails, return a fresh uniform vector. This helper is the sole restoration mechanism for the parent when needed, starts, perturbations, line-search proposals, and final output.

3.4. Implement a lag-vector helper returning a length-(2n−1) float64 vector in NumPy full-correlation order, using np.correlate(h, 1.0−h, mode='full') * dx. Implement an exact-score helper that first checks one-dimensional shape, finiteness, box bounds, and mass within 1e−10, then returns the Python float maximum of that scaled vector; invalid candidates return an invalid marker or positive infinity. This exact helper must be used for all candidate acceptance and final scoring. Also implement a feasibility predicate with the same checks.

3.5. Implement a coordinate-gradient-column helper from the formula in section 2. Given h and coordinate k, construct d = arange(−n+1,n), initialize a zero vector, add dx(1−h[k−d]) where 0≤k−d<n, and subtract dx h[k+d] where 0≤k+d<n. Use indexed addition so both terms combine correctly at d=0. A pair-direction helper obtains b by subtracting the two gradient columns and constructs q with the three nonzero entries specified in section 2. Compute a from the lag-vector helper. This avoids building a dense lag-by-coordinate gradient matrix.

3.6. Implement a generic feasible-alpha helper for zero-sum v. Start with lo=−infinity and hi=+infinity. For each i with vᵢ>0, update lo=max(lo,−hᵢ/vᵢ) and hi=min(hi,(1−hᵢ)/vᵢ). For each i with vᵢ<0, update lo=max(lo,(1−hᵢ)/vᵢ) and hi=min(hi,−hᵢ/vᵢ). Skip a zero direction or an interval of width at most 1e−14. For pair transfers use the explicit lo and hi formulas in section 2.

Implement one common line-search helper taking vectors a, b, q and finite lo≤0≤hi. Evaluate the line objective at 17 equally spaced points over [lo,hi] plus alpha=0, removing duplicate points. For a batch A of trial values, compute each value as max over lags of a + A b + A² q, using broadcasting rather than a loop over individual lags. Choose the smallest value, breaking ties by smaller |alpha|. Bracket the selected grid point by its immediate neighboring grid points, clipped to [lo,hi]. Repeat five times: evaluate five equally spaced points in the current bracket, update the best observed value and alpha, and narrow the bracket to the neighboring points around that round’s best. Retain the best over all rounds and the initial alpha=0. If any coefficients or evaluated values are nonfinite, return alpha=0. This is a deterministic approximate minimizer of the exact one-dimensional envelope, not a claim of globally exact line minimization. Candidate acceptance below always uses the full evaluator formula.

3.7. Build up to nine jointly feasible starts algorithmically. Include the feasible fallback; its reversal; its complement 1−h; one np.roll shift by max(1,n//3) when n>1; two independent Gaussian perturbations of the fallback with standard deviations 0.04 and 0.12 followed by projection; one seeded uniform [0,1] vector followed by projection; one near-binary vector; and one cosine vector when n≥2. Make the near-binary vector by permuting indices with the seeded generator, assigning floor(T) entries to 1, assigning T−floor(T) to one further entry when nonzero, and assigning 0 to the rest. Make the cosine vector as 0.5+0.45 cos(2π f(i+0.5)/n+phase), using a seeded phase uniform on [0,2π) and seeded integer f from 1 through min(4,floor(n/2)); then project. Project every generated start, skip invalid starts, and remove duplicates whose maximum coordinate difference is below 1e−12. Score all starts exactly and compare them with the fallback before searching.

3.8. Implement a pair-descent helper. For each sweep, create every unordered pair p<q, shuffle its order with the seeded generator, and process the pairs sequentially. For each pair, use the current h to compute a, b, q and the feasible interval; call the common line search. If its predicted line value does not beat the current exact score by at least 1e−12, skip the proposal. Otherwise form a trial by adding alpha to h[p] and subtracting alpha from h[q], jointly project it, check feasibility, and compute its exact full-correlation score. Accept it as the current state only if the exact score is lower than the current exact score by more than 1e−12. After every accepted move, replace a with the recomputed exact lag vector before processing the next pair. Preserve a copy of the best feasible candidate and its exact score independently of the current branch. After a full sweep, stop if the exact score fell by no more than 1e−10; otherwise continue. Use a maximum of four sweeps for an initial start and two sweeps for an escape start. A strict exact-score decrease prevents cycling from equal-score proposals.

3.9. Add a random-direction escape helper. For each requested direction, draw n independent standard normal values, subtract their mean, set the last entry to the negative sum of the preceding entries when n>1, and normalize by maximum absolute value. Skip a zero or nonfinite direction. This yields a numerically zero-sum direction; joint projection still corrects any residual mass drift. Compute its feasible alpha interval, a from the current exact lag vector, b=dx × (np.correlate(v,1−h,mode='full')−np.correlate(h,v,mode='full')), and q=−dx × np.correlate(v,v,mode='full'). Use the common line search, project the proposal, and accept only an exact score decrease greater than 1e−12. Recompute the current lag vector after acceptance. Try four random directions after the initial pair descent for each start; if any direction is accepted, run two more pair sweeps.

3.10. Run the search sequentially. For each deduplicated start, perform four pair sweeps, then the four-direction escape stage, then the conditional two-sweep refinement described above. Update the independent global best whenever a feasible candidate has a strictly smaller exact score. After all starts, perform three iterated escape rounds from the current global best, with Gaussian perturbation standard deviations 0.015, 0.05, and 0.15 in that order. In each round project best_h+sigma*noise, run two pair sweeps, try three random directions, and run one further pair sweep if any random direction was accepted. A worse branch never replaces the global best. All starts, sweeps, direction counts, line-grid evaluations, and escape rounds are fixed operations inside run; do not ask for external tuning or feedback.

3.11. Before returning, jointly project the stored best and the fallback, compute both exact scores, and return the lower-scoring feasible vector, retaining the fallback on a tie. If any check or calculation for the best fails, use the fallback; if the fallback itself is unusable, use a fresh uniform vector at the same n. Recompute the score from the final selected vector after all fallback selection.

4. Search choices and useful variations
The default is the parent resolution, normally n=47, with at most nine starts, four pair sweeps per start, a 17-point coarse line grid, five rounds of five-point refinement, four random directions per start, and the three final perturbation scales specified above. Use float64 and deterministic seeding throughout. Skip the exhaustive pair-search stages for n>64; never resample a parent merely to meet the search cap.

If the coder chooses a modest budget variation, useful ranges are 6–10 distinct starts, 2–6 pair sweeps, 13–25 coarse line points, 3–7 refinement rounds, and 2–8 random directions. Perturbation scales between 0.01 and 0.20 are reasonable; retain small, medium, and larger scales rather than using only one. The listed defaults need no preliminary experiments. Any added or removed start must be generated compactly and projected. Any result-dependent extra effort must follow explicit in-program rules, such as the specified shake after a stalled sweep; never treat a line-model improvement as acceptance without the exact score. Non-negotiable correctness requirements are the finite full correlation, all lags, the box and mass constraints, a validated parent fallback, and exact score comparison.

5. Numerical robustness and memory use
Use float64 throughout. Bound every accepted state by the joint projection and verify it; do not rely on solver tolerances or independent clipping and rescaling. Reject nonfinite parents and proposals before scoring. Use the uniform feasible vector if projection arithmetic fails on a finite extreme input. If a line coefficient or line evaluation is nonfinite, skip that move. A failed correlation or invalid score must not replace the stored best. There is no external solver in this design, so solver failure handling is unnecessary; every invalid helper result leaves the current state and fallback intact.

At n=47 there are 93 lags. A line-search batch contains at most 17 lag values, and a gradient column is only length 93; do not allocate a three-dimensional tensor or a dense Hessian. Memory is O(n) for vectors and starts, plus O(17n) for one line-search batch. Pair sweeps require O(n²) directions and O(n) work per direction, so cap exhaustive search at n=64 as specified. Run sequentially on the single available CPU with no parallel workers. Exact scoring uses the full np.correlate expression even when it is more expensive than the line-model calculations.

6. Runtime safeguards and return contract
All validation and optimization described in this plan must be implemented as program operations for the harness to execute. The program must check input dimensionality and finiteness, derive n and dx from runtime data, preserve a validated projected parent fallback, project every generated or accepted proposal onto 0≤hᵢ≤1 and Σhᵢ=n/2, and calculate each candidate score with max(np.correlate(h, 1−h, mode='full') * (2.0/n)). Do not use a circular correlation or a surrogate value for candidate selection or the returned score.

Return exactly a three-tuple (h_values, c5_bound, n_points): h_values is a one-dimensional float NumPy array of length n, c5_bound is a Python float recomputed from that returned array by the exact formula, and n_points is int(n). Ensure the final vector satisfies the box constraints and has mass within 1e−10 of n/2. If there is no exact improvement, return the best validated fallback or other feasible candidate already stored; if all candidate handling fails, return the uniform feasible vector. Do not fabricate a score or claim that the 0.3808 target was reached.
